content.text: Initial search terms seem too specific. Need to broaden the query to find foundational literature on evaluating predictive models, focusing on the distinction between in-sample and out-of-sample performance. The goal is to uncover papers that discuss the theoretical basis for separating these error components. Reframing the search to emphasize the conceptual challenges of assessing model performance using the data used for training.

The initial assessment focuses on distinguishing in-sample and out-of-sample performance, seeking literature on the theoretical basis for this separation. The specific example in the materials appears limited to in-sample calculation, failing to address broader concepts of generalization or held-out performance, such as optimism of training error or cross-validation techniques. Foundational literature related to the bias-variance tradeoff, and calibration on fitted samples versus held-out validation is relevant to this distinction.

I'm thinking through how to approach this.

Foundational papers highlight the distinction between in-sample and out-of-sample error, and how this relates to model assessment. These papers include Efron (1983) which defines optimism and Stone (1974) and Geisser (1975) which highlight out-of-sample prediction. The aim is to establish the theoretical background for evaluating prediction correction methods.

Apparent error rates on fitted data are biased due to over-optimism, as parameters are tuned to that specific sample. Cross-validation and covariance penalties correct for this bias by evaluating on held-out data or adjusting for model adaptation. The papers detail how cross-validation and similar techniques provide less biased estimates of generalization error by accounting for the degree to which a model is fit to the data.

These papers provide further insights into the complexities of model validation techniques. The work by Steyerberg et al. (2001) analyzes internal validation, addressing apparent performance, optimism, and calibration. Dwork et al. (2015) highlights the issue of holdout validity when used adaptively. Bates et al. (2023) examines what cross-validation actually estimates compared to in-sample model performance.

These works further solidify the need to assess models on independent data. The 1974 paper formalizes cross-validation as essential for determining prediction quality by evaluating observations not used in parameter estimation. The 1975 publication establishes sample reuse techniques to combat optimistic bias, preventing circularity in model assessment. The 1986 study provides formulas for the error bias inherent in in-sample error rates.

The 1995 paper explores the difference between in-sample and out-of-sample performance across sample sizes, providing empirical and theoretical insights. A 2004 study highlights the limitations of estimating variance in cross-validation due to sample dependencies. Further validation techniques are explored in the context of logistic regression, and how the reusable holdout issue impacts generalizability. The 2023 work clarifies the estimand and limits of hold-out performance assessment versus in-sample performance.
